content: Assisted vaginal births are performed to expedite delivery for the benefit of both the mother and the baby. However, these procedures can sometimes result in significant complications for either or both parties. Various instruments are used for assisted vaginal births, which are broadly categorized into forceps and vacuum cups. The choice of instrument is influenced by clinical circumstances, the operator's preference and experience, and the availability of the instruments. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of different instruments in achieving vaginal birth and to assess the associated risks of complications for both the mother and the baby. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different instruments for assisted vaginal birth. Trials with quasi-randomized designs, cluster-randomized designs, or cross-over designs were excluded. Abstract-only trials were included if sufficient information was available to assess eligibility. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis, and the GRADE approach was applied to assess the certainty of the evidence. The primary outcomes evaluated included failed delivery with the allocated instrument, maternal trauma, thirdand fourth-degree perineal tears, postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), neonatal trauma, low Apgar scores, and low umbilical artery pH. The review included 31 studies involving 5,754 women. The risk of bias was generally assessed as unclear due to insufficient detail in the trial reports. Blinding was not feasible in these trials because the type of instrument used could not be concealed from either the operator or the patient. Forceps vs. Vacuum Cups Forceps were less likely to fail in achieving vaginal birth compared to vacuum cups (low-certainty evidence). Maternal trauma, including thirdand fourth-degree perineal tears, was more likely with forceps (low-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in the incidence of postpartum hemorrhage between the two groups, but the evidence was imprecise due to wide confidence intervals (low-certainty evidence). More women in the forceps group required pain relief. There was no significant difference in the rates of low Apgar scores or low umbilical artery pH between the two groups (moderateto low-certainty evidence). Fetal trauma, including cephalhematoma, retinal hemorrhage, and jaundice, was less common with forceps. However, the composite outcome of any neonatal trauma was not reported. Low-Cavity Forceps vs. Vacuum Cups Two small studies with 218 participants were included in this comparison. Most of the evidence was of very low certainty, making it difficult to draw conclusions about differences in failed delivery rates, maternal trauma, or thirdand fourth-degree tears. Postpartum hemorrhage and low umbilical artery pH were not reported. Soft Vacuum Cups vs. Rigid Vacuum Cups Failed delivery was more likely with soft vacuum cups compared to rigid vacuum cups (low-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in maternal trauma or thirdand fourth-degree tears between the two groups, but the evidence was imprecise (low-certainty evidence). There was probably no difference in the rates of postpartum hemorrhage between the two groups (moderate-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in the rates of low Apgar scores or low umbilical artery pH between the two groups (low-certainty evidence). Handheld Vacuum Cups vs. Other Vacuum Cups There was no significant difference in the rates of failed delivery, maternal trauma, postpartum hemorrhage, low Apgar scores, or low umbilical artery pH between handheld vacuum cups and other vacuum cups (low-certainty evidence). There was probably no difference in the rates of thirdand fourth-degree tears between the two groups (moderate-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions The review provides low-certainty evidence that forceps may be more effective in achieving vaginal birth and may result in lower rates of fetal trauma compared to vacuum cups. However, forceps are associated with a higher risk of perineal trauma and greater need for pain relief. Rigid vacuum cups may be more effective than soft vacuum cups in achieving vaginal birth but are associated with higher rates of fetal trauma. Handheld vacuum cups appear to have similar success rates compared to other vacuum cups. There was no significant difference in the rates of thirdand fourth-degree tears or postpartum hemorrhage between different types of vacuum cups, but the wide confidence intervals suggest that further research is needed in this area.
